attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own essay, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense observation about generative AI providers as a class. The normalised wording keeps the scope and adds no quantifier.

contract.note: Reading it as a class-level serving-cost claim is ordinary. But 'said costs' could also point back to training and talent costs. Zitron gave no cost basis, so the result depends on serving contribution versus fully allocated profit.

evidence.note: Altman says the Pro plan is unprofitable. That covers one plan at one provider around Dec 2024 to Jan 2025, so it cannot show the result for paying customers as a class across providers.

Secondary report of an internal OpenAI metric, from an anonymous source: 52% paid-user compute margin at end of 2024. This is strong counterevidence on a serving-cost reading, but it is not a matched disclosure and leaves out fully allocated costs.

reviews.rationale: On a serving-cost reading, e9 suggests OpenAI's paid users covered compute in late 2024, which cuts against the claim. On a fully allocated reading it does not. The evidence is one anonymous-sourced secondary report and one single-plan statement, with no matched provider records for Q4 2024, so the packet does not settle the claim on a specified basis.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: 'Guaranteeing it'll lose billions more' is a firm forecast. 'Appears to be' hedges only the continuation premise. The moat part is a bundled present observation.

contract.note: Reading 'billions more' as at least $2B with no deadline is ordinary. Scoring the bundle by component is fair. Moat durability is unspecified, so that part depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own release notice shows it kept selling language models after publication (GPT-5 API, Aug 2025). This bears on the condition only.

Reported 2025 figures: net loss near $39B, about $8B excluding a one-off charge, operating loss about $20.9B. The year includes about 55 days before publication, but the post-publication losses plainly exceed $2B.
Microsoft describes the partnership and Azure API exclusivity. That does not establish a durable moat outside the stated exceptions; Zitron himself counts compute access via Microsoft.

reviews.rationale: Loss forecast holds. The 2025 losses reported in e2 meet the early-resolution rule of at least $2B in additional losses after publication while the LLM business continued (e1), even after allowing for the pre-publication weeks. The moat observation and the causal explanation are not settled: e3 shows a partnership, not a proven durable advantage either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: Universal 'every single paying customer' is kept, 'somehow' is kept, and 'not a real company' is rhetorical. Observation is the right kind.

contract.note: Reading 'loses money on a customer' as each customer's attributable costs exceeding their revenue is ordinary. Zitron's own support divides company-wide costs, so the cost-allocation choice decides the result.

evidence.note: A 52% paid-user compute margin in late 2024 strongly undercuts 'every single' customer losing money. But it covers compute only, a narrower cost category the contract excludes. The metric_scope 'net' label is wrong: this is a gross margin.
Reports company-wide expected 2024 losses and Altman's statement that the Pro plan loses money. Neither shows customer-level losses across all paying customers or subscriber-driven burn.

reviews.rationale: No customer-level or cohort profit evidence and no analysis of extra burn from additional subscribers. The positive compute margin in e1 casts serious doubt on the universal claim, but under the contract it is compute-only and cannot contradict it. Company-wide losses and one unprofitable plan cannot support it. 'Not a real company' is rhetoric and is not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own concluding sentence, introduced as 'The point I am making'.

semantics.note: The wording is faithful, but this is a polemical characterisation. It names no specific representation, and its main example (calling LLMs 'AI') is a contested definitional judgment, not a checkable fact.

contract.note: Turning an op-ed charge into a fraud test that needs knowing falsity and investor-reliance records stretches the plain words. Whether calling LLMs 'AI' is a lie depends on definitions Zitron did not supply.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement confirms an Oct 2024 fundraise. It says nothing about false capability claims.
OpenAI publicly disclosed GPT-4's hallucinations in 2023. This bears on concealment but cannot settle the charge of deceptive marketing.

reviews.rationale: The claim is evaluative rhetoric: it names no specific false statement or fundraising event, and its central example (the term 'artificial intelligence') is a definitional dispute. Neither item can test it; both are context only.
